paper_title: Training the Whole Agent, Not Just the Model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Training coding agents typically updates the policy while keeping the harness fixed. During training, trajectories reveal flawed repair strategies and interaction problems that vary across tasks and change as the policy learns. We introduce HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains the policy and adapts its harness during reinforcement learning. For flawed repair strategies, a frozen teacher generates task-specific mechanism-level skills. For interaction problems recurring across tasks, a separate teacher model evolves tools and hooks, keeping each change only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. The policy trains with the adapted harness, and its new trajectories guide further adaptation. With a 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, and outperforms GRPO with the human-designed OpenHands harness. Gains from mechanism-level skills persist after their removal at evaluation. Re-evolving tools and hooks as the policy changes outperforms freezing early versions. Removing them at deployment, in contrast, costs up to 7.7 percentage points. Training therefore produces a model-harness pair: the trained policy and the evolved tools and hooks, with skills removed at deployment.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: A coding agent operates as modelharness pair: the model selects actions, while the harness provides guidance, tools, and runtime feedback. Agent training typically improves the policy while keeping the harness fixed [13]. The harness shapes the interaction trajectories used to update the policy, affecting both the effectiveness of training and the performance of the trained agent [4]. Prior work has explored both harness optimization and training-time guidance. Previous methods optimize the harness while keeping the policy fixed [57]. Other methods use skills and training guidance to improve policy learning from trajectories [810]. Co-Harness alternates harness updates with supervised fine-tuning on trajectories generated by the improved harness [4]. We study harness adaptation during reinforcement learning for coding agents. During training, trajectories expose flawed repair strategies, such as incorrect diagnoses or fixes that only address symptoms. They also reveal interaction problems, such as failed editing commands, excessive output, or insufficient verification. This evidence can guide changes to skills, tools, and runtime hooks that help alleviate these problems. As the problems vary across tasks and change with the policy, the harness needs to adapt throughout training (Appendix C.3). We therefore ask how to design skills for policy learning, how to design and select tools and hooks as the policy changes, and which harness components to retain at deployment. To address these questions, we introduce HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains the policy and adapts its harness during reinforcement learning. In our setting, skills are textual guidance supplied to the policy during training. First, we compare three skill-guidance variants and use mechanism-level skills that explain when and why repair strategy applies without providing concrete answers. frozen teacher model generates these taskWork is done during internship at LIGHTSPEED. Second, separate teacher model identifies recurring interaction and feedback problems across tasks and proposes changes to tools and hooks. Harness selection considers both task success and the availability of rollouts for policy updates (Section 3.3). Each proposal is kept only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either (Appendix B.2). We refer to this process as tool and hook evolution. The policy then trains with GRPO [11] on fresh rollouts using the evolved tools and hooks and skills for assisted tasks. Trajectories from the updated policy guide later proposals. Third, we examine which components should remain at deployment. We evaluate the policy after removing skills and compare performance with and without the evolved tools and hooks. With 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified [12], Multilingual [2], and Pro [13]. It also outperforms GRPO training with the human-designed OpenHands harness on all three benchmarks. Under the same base harness, models trained with mechanism-level skills perform best among the three skill-guidance variants when evaluated without skills. Re-evolving tools and hooks as the policy changes outperforms keeping their early versions fixed. Holding the trained policy weights fixed, removing the evolved tools and hooks at evaluation reduces pass@1 by up to 7.7 percentage points. Together, these results show that gains from skills persist after their removal, while the evolved tools and hooks remain necessary for full performance at deployment. Our contributions are threefold: Skill design for policy learning. We compare three skill-guidance variants and find that mechanism-level skills yield the best repair performance after guidance is removed. Tool and hook evolution during reinforcement learning. We use current-policy trajectories to propose tools and hooks and select changes using both the pass rate and the trainable rate. Training and deploying the modelharness pair. We show that gains from skill guidance persist after its removal, while retaining the evolved tools and hooks at deployment preserves the complete performance.

sections.title: 3.1 Policy-Adaptive Repair Skills
sections.content: We generate skills from training trajectories to guide the policys repair strategies. Prior work finds that many skills do not improve software engineering performance [16]. We therefore compare three ways of generating skills and assess the models performance after training, with the skills removed. We first evaluate skill bank with fixed capacity, based on prior work that extracts reusable strategies from trajectories [17, 18]. The teacher reviews trajectories across training tasks and adds, removes, merges, or updates general repair skills. This approach does not consistently improve performance over GRPO, suggesting that these skills are too general to help with individual repair tasks (Section 4.3). more taskspecific alternative is to provide near-answer hints with concrete code changes, including variable, function, or class names. These hints produce shorter trajectories and higher training success, but the trained model performs worse than GRPO when evaluated without them (Section 4.3, Appendix C.2). We therefore propose mechanism-level skills that focus on the policys flawed repair strategies while leaving the policy to work out the concrete solution. For each assisted task, the teacher model compares two trajectories from the current policy. Using the issue and the evidence in these trajectories, it identifies repair strategy and explains when and why it applies. The resulting mechanism-level skill retains the technical reasoning behind the repair but omits repository paths, code symbols, and literal code. This guides the policys repair strategy while leaving code localization and implementation to the policy. Appendices A.2 and D.2 provide generation details and examples.

sections.title: 3.2 Evolving Tools and Hooks for Policy Training
sections.content: Training trajectories also reveal recurring problems in how the policy interacts with its environment. The teacher uses this evidence to propose changes to tools and hooks. To support both task performance and policy learning, it uses the pass rate and the trainable rate to guide these proposals. Trainable rollouts are those usable for policy updates (Appendix B.2). The teacher uses current-policy trajectories and the current harness to develop proposal in four steps. (1) 3 Find recurring problems. The teacher compares trajectories across tasks to identify recurring problems in tool use and feedback. (2) Inspect trajectories. The teacher reads the tool calls, outputs, and hook messages to understand each recurring problem. For example, the policy runs fewer verification tests later in training, even though it has testing tools and receives reminders. The teacher inspects these trajectories to understand why the policy skips tests before submitting patch. (3) Design changes. To address the identified problems, the teacher can propose one or more tools, hooks, or combination of both. Tools package repair operations into reusable actions. Hooks give the policy feedback during execution. In the testing example, the teacher modifies the patch-preparation tool so that it automatically runs related tests when preparing patch. hook then reports any test failures and reminds the policy to check them before submission. (4) Implement the proposal. The teacher implements the proposed changes as candidate harness for evaluation. As the policy learns, its new trajectories guide further adaptation of tools and hooks (Appendix C.3). Appendix B.2 provides the full proposal procedure.

sections.title: 3.3 Training-Aware Harness Selection
sections.content: We select harness changes to support both task success and policy learning. GRPO uses reward differences among attempts on the same task to update the policy [11, 19]. Groups in which all attempts succeed or all fail provide no reward contrast for policy updates. Successful rollouts in an all-success group therefore count toward the pass rate without contributing to policy learning. To account for training usability, we also measure the trainable rate, the fraction of sampled rollouts eligible for policy updates (Appendix B.2). We evaluate each proposal by running the candidate and current harnesses with the same policy, tasks, skills, and rollout budget. We accept the proposal only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. These rates are empirical fractions from the finite comparison rollouts; the acceptance rule does not test statistical significance. Accepted changes are used for subsequent policy training. Otherwise, training continues with the current tools and hooks. Changes from rejected proposal can be proposed again in later rounds. Policy updates. After selection, we collect fresh rollouts with the selected tools and hooks, providing skills for assisted tasks. Preparation and comparison rollouts are not reused for training. We update the policy with GRPO using the new rollouts, with loss computed only on policy-generated tokens [11]. Evolution across training epochs. Each training epoch begins with up to five rounds of tool and hook evolution. After each round, we update the policy using the selected tools and hooks. These tools and hooks then stay fixed for the remaining training steps in that epoch. The first epoch produces H1. The second epoch starts from H1 and uses trajectories from the updated policy to evolve H2.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Training setup. We train on fixed subset of the R2E-Gym-Lite training split [1], shared across all training configurations. The training tasks are disjoint from the evaluation benchmarks. In HarnessAdapt-RL, skills are provided for all training tasks in the first epoch and fixed subset in the second. Appendix A.1 details task selection and the assisted subset. Our base model is Qwen3.5-9B [20], and the base harness H0 uses mini-swe-agent [15]. We use the frozen GLM-5.3-Flash teacher [21] to generate skills, and GPT-5.6 Sol [22] through Codex [23] to propose and implement tools and hooks. Appendix B.1 records the model identifiers and access interfaces. Policy training uses GRPO [11]. submitted patch receives reward of 1 if it passes the task tests and 0 otherwise. The GRPO baseline receives twice as many policy-training rollouts as the other trained configurations. Appendix gives implementation details and hyperparameters, and Appendix C.7 reports the additional costs of preparation, harness comparison, and teacher calls. 4 Configurations. Base model uses the initial policy and base harness H0 without training. GRPO trains the policy with H0 and no skills. OpenHands-GRPO uses the human-designed OpenHands harness, also without skills [24]. To compare three ways of generating skills, Skill-Hint, Skill-Mechanism, and Skill-Bank use near-answer hints, mechanism-level skills, and general repair skills from skill bank, respectively. All three train the policy with the base harness H0. We compare three further configurations to test whether tools and hooks need to adapt as the policy learns. All three use mechanism-level skills during policy training. Our full method, HarnessAdapt-RL, alternates policy updates with tool and hook evolution in both epochs. Pre-Evolved tests whether evolving tools and hooks before policy training is enough. It follows the same search steps and uses the same tasks as HarnessAdapt-RL. However, the policy stays fixed at the base model throughout the search. It then trains the policy for two epochs with the resulting harness Hpre fixed. H1+Mechanism tests whether tools and hooks need to evolve again in the second epoch. It shares the first epoch with HarnessAdapt-RL, so both start the second epoch with the same policy checkpoint and harness H1. Both continue training the policy, but H1+Mechanism keeps H1 fixed, while HarnessAdapt-RL evolves it into H2. Appendix C.6 reports additional fixed-harness configurations. Evaluation. We report pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified [12, 25], SWE-bench Multilingual [2], and SWEbench Pro [13]. Each evaluation run uses one attempt per task. We repeat each evaluation three times and report the mean pass@1. We assess statistical significance using paired bootstrap confidence intervals for performance differences (Appendix C.4). All configurations use the same evaluation limits (Appendix A.3). Evaluation uses no skills, teacher assistance, or further harness updates. Table 1 compares complete agents, each evaluated with its deployment harness.

sections.title: 4.3 Why Mechanism-Level Skills?
sections.content: Figure 2 shows that skill-bank training closely follows GRPO in both training success and Verified performance. This suggests that its general repair strategies offer limited help for individual tasks. Near-answer hints increase training success substantially, but the trained model performs worse than GRPO after skills are removed. Mechanism-level skills improve training success while also achieving the best performance without skills. Higher success during training does not necessarily lead to better performance after training. To examine this difference, we first compare the rewards of attempts on the same task. GRPO uses these reward differences to update the policy [11, 19]. When every attempt succeeds or every attempt fails, the rewards cannot distinguish better attempts. With mechanism-level skills, 46.5% of sampled groups contain both successful and failed attempts, compared with 39.0% with near-answer hints. The latter produce more groups in which every attempt succeeds (Appendix C.1). Their higher success rate therefore also comes with more groups that provide no reward difference for learning. Figure 2 Training success and Verified performance without skills. Faint lines show individual updates, bold lines five-update trailing means; dashed lines separate the two training epochs. Providing concrete answers also changes what the policy needs to do during training. These answers allow it to skip many steps required for independent repair, including locating the relevant code and deciding how to modify it. Providing concrete answers reduces the average number of tokens per rollout by 40.8% relative to 6 GRPO, compared with 14.5% for mechanism-level skills. The trajectories are much shorter. However, they can leave out too many steps needed to solve the task independently. At evaluation, the policy must complete these steps without assistance. The model trained with concrete answers performs worse than GRPO after skills are removed (Appendix C.2).

sections.title: 4.4 How Do Tools and Hooks Evolve During Training?
sections.content: Figure 3 reports the relative changes in pass rate and trainable rate for each candidate compared with the current harness. Early evolution targets context management and patch submission. Reading and search tools limit the text returned in each call, preserving context for later repair steps. Editing tools apply changes directly, reducing the need for shell commands that can fail because of quoting or syntax errors. The first proposal containing these tools raises the pass rate by 13.7% and the trainable rate by 7.4%. Later proposals add tools that generate patches and display code changes, helping the policy prepare and check its submission. Hooks flag repeated actions and remind the policy to reserve steps for checking and submission. The accepted changes form H1  (Table 12)  . Figure 3 Relative changes (%) in pass rate and trainable rate for each candidate compared with the current harness in the same round. Later evolution focuses on testing and revising repairs. With H1 kept fixed, the policy runs fewer verification tests in the second epoch despite having testing tool and reminders (Appendix C.3). The teacher adds automatic testing to the tool that prepares the patch. It selects and runs tests related to the changed code. hook reports failures and reminds the policy to inspect them before submission. This proposal raises the pass rate by 6.3% and the trainable rate by 7.4%. Revised budget reminders discourage repeatedly running every test in the repository while still encouraging tests for the current repair. Another proposal helps the policy undo unsuccessful edits. When Git command for undoing changes is blocked, hook recommends the new restore_file tool. This tool restores one file to its original version while preserving edits to other files, so the policy does not have to discard its other work. sections.title: 4.6 Can the Evolved Harness Be Reused for Training?
sections.content: We compare reusing H2 with searching for harness before policy training. Frozen-H2+Mechanism reuses H2 discovered by HarnessAdapt-RL. PreEvolved instead searches with the base policy fixed, using the same search steps and tasks as HarnessAdapt-RL. After obtaining their harnesses, both variants train new policy from the same base model. Their tools and hooks remain fixed throughout training. We provide mechanism-level skills on the same schedule as in the full method (Section 4.1). Frozen-H2+Mechanism reaches 56.8%, 38.3%, and 38.9% on Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, respectively. These scores are within 1.0 percentage point of HarnessAdapt-RL on every benchmark (Figure 4). They also exceed Pre-Evolved by 1.6, 5.3, and 1.9 percentage points. Thus, reusing the harness discovered during policy training gives better results than using the harness found before training. Figure 4 Pass@1 differences (percentage points) from HarnessAdapt-RL. Frozen-H2+Mechanism and Pre-Evolved both train with fixed harnesses and mechanism-level skills, then remove skills at evaluation. Frozen-H2+Mechanism achieves similar scores to HarnessAdapt-RL. However, it reuses harness that HarnessAdapt-RL has already discovered during policy training. In our experiments, searching with the fixed base policy does not produce harness with the same performance. The strong reuse result therefore depends on first discovering H2 through evolution during training. Once H2 is available, this evolution does not need to be repeated in the new training run.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Skills and policy learning. Voyager builds reusable skills from interaction [26], while SkillRL combines skill evolution with reinforcement learning [18]. Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) maintains playbook of strategies and updates it using feedback from the agents interactions [27]. Socratic-SWE uses skills derived from trajectories to generate training tasks [8]. Hindsight Hint Distillation trains on trajectories generated with hints, while PATS adjusts guidance to the current policy [9, 10]. Both remove this guidance at deployment. We compare near-answer hints, mechanism-level skills, and general skills from skill bank in software repair. Our comparison focuses on the trained models performance after skills are removed. Harness design and optimization. Tool interfaces and feedback affect agent behavior [15, 28, 29]. MetaHarness automates harness search using earlier candidates and their execution trajectories [5]. Retrospective Harness Optimization (RHO) updates skills and tools from past trajectories, selecting changes through the agents own preferences without external grading [30]. Other methods use revision history, reference trajectories, or interactions across tasks to guide changes [6, 7, 31]. These methods keep model weights fixed during harness optimization. We evolve tools and hooks during policy training. The teacher uses trajectories from the updated policy to propose changes for newly observed problems. Our experiments compare this approach with search under fixed base policy. Policy training and harness adaptation. CoEvolve adapts training data alongside the policy [32], while SEARL jointly optimizes the policy and tool graph memory [33]. ClawGym II studies reinforcement learning with complex harnesses [34]. Co-Harness alternates harness updates with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on trajectories generated by the improved harness [4]. HarnessAdapt-RL combines GRPO with tool and hook selection based on the pass rate and trainable rate. proposal is accepted only if at least one observed rate improves and neither decreases. We also examine which components are needed at deployment. We test whether skill gains persist after removal and how removing the evolved tools and hooks affects performance.

sections.content: We introduced HarnessAdapt-RL, which trains coding agents with GRPO and adapts their harnesses from It generates task-specific skills and evolves tools and hooks as the policy learns. training trajectories. proposal is accepted only if it improves the observed pass rate or the observed trainable rate without lowering either. With 9B base model, HarnessAdapt-RL improves pass@1 over GRPO by 9.8, 12.6, and 6.4 percentage points on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro. It also outperforms OpenHands-GRPO. Mechanism-level skills outperform near-answer hints and general skills from skill bank after skills are removed. Evolving tools and hooks during policy training performs better than searching only before training or keeping the first-epoch harness fixed. Once discovered, the evolved harness can support new training run without further evolution. Removing its tools and hooks at deployment lowers pass@1 by up to 7.7 percentage points. Training therefore produces modelharness pair: the trained policy and the evolved tools and hooks, with task-specific skills removed at deployment.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: All tasks are software repair from SWE-bench-style benchmarks, and the skills, tools, and hooks were derived for this setting. We have not tested whether the same procedure produces useful support in other agent 9 domains, such as web navigation or data analysis. We also use single 9B base model. We do not know whether larger models, which may already handle many of the operations that our tools package, would benefit from harness evolution to the same extent, or whether the preferred form of guidance would stay the same across model families. Each configuration is trained once. The three repetitions are evaluations of fixed trained checkpoint, not independent training runs (Appendix B.4). The reported confidence intervals characterize task-level variation for these checkpoints; they do not quantify variability across training seeds or independent harness-search runs. Candidate selection uses observed pass and trainable rates from finite rollout comparison (Appendix B.2). Its acceptance rule is not significance test: an observed improvement need not imply an improvement in the underlying success or trainability probabilities. Rollout noise and repeated candidate search can therefore affect which changes are retained. The statistical analysis of the final evaluations does not remove this uncertainty from the search process.

sections.title: A Data and Harness Specifications
sections.content: A.1 Task Pool and Assisted Subset We draw the training pool from the train split of R2E-Gym-Lite [1], which contains 4,578 tasks. We first remove tasks with pass@4 of 100%, then randomly sample 1,058 of the remaining tasks and use this pool for every training configuration. Table 3 reports its repository distribution. Repository Tasks Share Repository Tasks Share pandas numpy orange3 pillow aiohttp 399 37.71% tornado 163 15.41% scrapy 124 11.72% datalad 122 11.53% coveragepy 76 7.18% pyramid 62 5.86% 51 4.82% 31 2.93% 24 2.27% 6 0.57% Total The 512-task assisted subset is drawn uniformly at random from the pool, without reference to task difficulty, and is held fixed across configurations. For configurations with skills, the first epoch assists all 1,058 tasks and the second assists only this subset. Skill-Gated further restricts guidance to tasks whose preparation attempts all fail. Tasks outside the subset keep the current harness but receive no skill. We deduplicate the training pool against SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro and find no overlap. Tasks are visited in the same order in every configuration. Table 3 Repository distribution of the training pool. 1,058 100% A.2 Skill Generation Teacher inputs. Each assisted task visit starts skill-generation request, which returns Markdown response. The teacher sees the issue and trajectory records, including any source code and test output shown in those records. It has no direct repository access and cannot inspect hidden tests or grader artifacts  (Table 4)  . Only the resulting skill is shown to the policy, and neither the teacher nor any training skill is used at evaluation. For mechanism-level skills, the skill describes the repair mechanism rather than reproducing the diff. Input Issue Trajectories Tests Direct repository access Hidden tests, grader artifacts Trajectory pairing. The teacher compares two of the four preparation rollouts of task, preferably one success and one failure. When all rollouts succeed, the pair consists of two successes and the skill describes the shared successful mechanism. When all rollouts fail, the pair consists of two failures, and the teacher decides from the issue and the partial progress in the trajectories which repair direction the skill describes. The skill format is the same in all three cases. Visible to the teacher Use Yes, as the user message in both trajectories Two full preparation trajectory records, with outcomes Only commands and outputs inside the two trajectories No No direct access States what the repair must accomplish Behavioral comparison Evidence the policy actually observed Table 4 Teacher inputs for skill generation. Guidance variants. The three variants differ in both specificity and evidence scope. Near-answer hints name the file, function, and variables involved and state the concrete edit. Each mechanism-level skill describes 14 single repair mechanism, with repository names, paths, symbols, literal code, and diff text removed. Both are generated from single task, using its issue and the two trajectories with the test outputs they contain. Skill-bank guidance instead summarizes general procedures that recur across tasks. The teacher reads the task reports from the current batch together with the previous meta-skill bank and rewrites the bank into at most ten procedures within 1,000 English words. Evidence identifiers are removed before the bank is shown to the policy. Section 4.3 compares the training and evaluation results of these variants. For Skill-Mechanism, only the Task-specific Skill section of the teachers response is injected. Appendix D.1 gives the full prompts for all three variants. Representative outputs. Appendix D.2 shows representative teacher outputs for each guidance type. Length and leakage control. Excluding the three field labels, mechanism-level skills average 100.67 whitespace-delimited words, with median of 100 and maximum of 154. We screen mechanism-level skills for answer-locating paths, symbols, and code. Near-answer hints intentionally include such details and are not subject to this restriction. mechanism-level skill that fails the screen is regenerated up to three times. If it still fails, the task is trained without skill. Second epoch and Skill-Gated. Skills for the second epoch are regenerated rather than reused from the first. Skill-Gated invokes the teacher only when all four preparation attempts of task fail, and generates the skill from two of these failed trajectories chosen at random. A.3 Execution Limits and Submission All configurations share the same execution budgets. Training rollouts allow 64K context (65,536 tokens) and at most 60 turns, while evaluation allows 128K context (131,072 tokens) and at most 150 turns. Both use temperature 1.0. The shorter training budget bounds the cost of collecting multiple rollouts per task for each GRPO update. Evaluation makes single attempt per held-out task, so the longer budget leaves the trained policy room to read, verify, and submit. Prior SWE agents also use shorter context or turn budgets during training than at evaluation [35, 36]. Shorter interaction horizons can also improve reinforcement-learning stability [37]. Truncation and submission. trajectory is truncated if it exceeds either the turn limit or the context limit, and is counted once if it exceeds both. submission made on the final allowed turn counts as complete. The prepare_patch tool writes the selected source changes to patch.txt but neither submits nor scores the repair. Submission is separate Bash action: echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT && cat patch.txt The submitted patch is then applied and tested in fresh task container.

sections.title: B Implementation and Reproducibility
sections.content: B.1 Hyperparameters and Schedule Policy training uses GRPO implemented in slime [38], with constant learning rate of 106. GLM-5.3Flash [21] generates skills through OpenCode [39], and GPT-5.6 Sol [22] designs and implements tool and hook proposals through Codex [23]. The release configuration records the provider model identifiers glm-5.3-flash and gpt-5.6-sol. The setup guide describes the provider endpoints and credentials used by the two CLIs; inference with the released modelH2 pair requires neither teacher. These identifiers do not pin immutable teacher snapshots, and the historical CLI package versions were not preserved. The reproduction setup therefore requires explicit CLI versions to be supplied and records the installed versions. Training runs for two epochs over the 1,058-task pool. Each epoch consists of 23 updates of 46 tasks (23 46 = 1,058), so every batch is full and no task is repeated or padded within an epoch. Updates 123 15 form the first epoch and updates 2446 the second, for 2,116 task visits in total. The first epoch assists all tasks, and the second assists the fixed 512-task subset with regenerated skills. GRPO samples 8 rollouts per task, and every other trained configuration samples 4. Each update therefore uses 368 training rollouts for GRPO and 184 for the other configurations, or 16,928 and 8,464 rollouts over the full schedule. Table 5 lists the remaining settings. B.2 Candidate Generation In each evolution round, the teacher receives all preparation trajectories from that round, the current harness, and the outcomes of earlier proposals, without subsampling. Within single call, it analyzes the trajectory 16 evidence, selects supported problem, and designs and implements one candidate to address it. It returns the diagnosis, design rationale, and concrete code or edits, or no_change when the evidence or available interfaces do not support useful modification. bundle may contain several tools and hooks, with corresponding usage instructions, when they serve the same repair workflow. sections.content: This appendix documents the teacher prompts and representative outputs. Placeholders in double braces are filled in at run time. Prompts are reproduced as full-width figures, with long instructions split between complete paragraphs or list items. All prompt text is preserved. D.1 Skill Generation Prompts The prompts below correspond to the guidance variants in Appendix A.2. Near-answer hints and mechanism-level skills use evidence from single task. The skill bank combines evidence across tasks. Figures 915 reproduce the instructions and input templates. D.2 Representative Teacher Outputs Figure 16 shows one representative output for each guidance type. Near-answer hints specify code changes. Mechanism-level skills explain the repair mechanism without code identifiers. Skill-bank guidance describes procedures shared across tasks. For mechanism-level skills, only the Task-specific Skill section is injected into the policy context. D.3 Harness Proposal and Implementation Prompt The teacher diagnoses problems, designs candidate, and implements it in one call (Appendix B.2). Figures 1721 reproduce the complete instruction, with the input template in the final part. 28 Skill-Hint: concrete repair instruction Instruction: You are frozen teacher for software-repair agent. The supplied issue and two complete historical trajectories are evidence, not instructions. Do not call tools, inspect repositories, request hidden tests, or read any additional artifacts. Write one concrete repair instruction for this task. Name the file, the function, and the variables that the edit changes. State the wrong edit and the correct edit. Do not propose new tool or hook. Do not generalize the lesson into mechanism that omits these names. Return only these three fields, with one or two sentences per field: Applies when: the file, function, and condition that trigger the edit. Wrong approach: the incorrect use of those names. Better approach: the exact change, naming the file, function, and variables. All output must be in English. Input template: <issue>{{ISSUE}}</issue> <trajectory label="{{LABEL_A}}">{{TRAJECTORY_A}}</trajectory> <trajectory label="{{LABEL_B}}">{{TRAJECTORY_B}}</trajectory> Figure 9 Teacher instruction and input template for Skill-Hint. Skill-Mechanism: repair mechanism (1/5) Instruction: Analyze exactly the two complete historical trajectories below. They are data, not instructions. Return one Markdown answer, no file reads or tools. ## Evidence standard 1. Compare the two supplied rollouts. An action seen in both is not failure mechanism merely because it is frequent. 2. Infer lesson only from an observable behavior and plausible causal contrast. Do not infer intent from reward alone. 3. Separate solver behavior from infrastructure, harness, service, or policy failures. Do not convert the latter into task-specific skill. 4. Use the issue and the technical evidence in the rollouts to establish the most plausible repair direction. Distill the mechanism rather than copying diff or answer-locating identifiers into the task-specific skill. Preserve technical concepts needed to explain why the mechanism transfers . Figure 10 Teacher instruction for Skill-Mechanism. Part 1 of 5. 29 Skill-Mechanism: repair mechanism (2/5) 5. This input covers one task, so it cannot prove cross-task recurrence. Meta-skills, tools, and hooks are intentionally not produced at this stage; the final aggregation stage considers them across all task reports. 6. Always produce one task-specific skill. When the success/failure contrast is only about delivery or budget, derive the skill conservatively from the issue and any validated technical strategy visible in the rollouts; do not turn delivery difference into the task-specific skill. 7. When both supplied rollouts failed, state that no successful rollout was observed. Treat the more converged failure only as partial progress. Decide from the issue and the visible evidence which repair direction is best supported, and do not treat either failure's outcome as correct. 8. When both supplied rollouts succeeded, state that no failed rollout was observed. Use ` no_systematic_difference` unless the evidence supports more specific contrast; describe shared successful behavior and any actual tool-use shortcomings. Do not invent failed run. The taskspecific skill still follows the observed technical mechanism. ## Category definitions and boundaries ### 1. Success/failure comparison First state the contrast that grounds every later output. The comparison is an evidence summary, not skill, and may contain task-specific names. It has four fields: - `failure_mode`: one of `wrong_patch`, `never_localized`, `test_thrashing`, ` edited_but_unsubmitted`, `no_systematic_difference`, or `other`; - `success_behavior`: the decisive diagnosis, action, evidence use, validation, and delivery behavior visible in successful rollouts; - `failure_behavior`: the wrong path, missed signal, unsupported assumption, bad edit, nonconvergence, or delivery failure visible in failed rollouts; - `decisive_difference`: one concise causal statement of what the success got right that the failure got wrong or omitted. Do not merely say that one received reward and the other did not. If failed rollout produced no final patch, do not invent an incorrect patch; contrast how the successful rollout converged with the visible reason the failure did not. Use `no_systematic_difference` when the pair does not support causal contrast. For failure-only pair, write explicitly that no successful rollout was observed, summarize the stronger partial progress under `success_behavior`, and contrast the two failure paths under the remaining fields. Figure 11 Teacher instruction for Skill-Mechanism. Part 2 of 5. Skill-Mechanism: repair mechanism (3/5) ### 2. Tool-use problems Identify shortcomings in how the model used tools and capabilities already available in either the successful or failed trajectory. successful rollout may still expose tool-use problems; success does not erase inefficient, incorrect, or risky tool behavior. This section is strictly about tool interaction, not general critique of reasoning style or task planning. Its findings are evidence for the final aggregation stage, not proposals for new tools or hooks.
